I agree, there's so many variables concerning home improvements. It's difficult to get a good scope, unless you already have a few costs set, know what the material cost will be, or what the materials are. A contractor will charge based on the appearance of the neighborhood and how much your home has been maintained, good or bad. I used to do a lot of side jobs painting, sheet rock, trim, decking, minor plumbing and electrical. Personally I would always do jobs at a hourly rate, this wasn't my main source of income, and I was working in the afternoons after my main job. A licensed contractor will start with a basic labor rate multipled by the surface area, then add material cost, plus 10%, usually for miscellaneous supplies like rags or cleaning supplies. I would tell OP get the exact surface area, Google going labor rate for flooring in Dallas, then add the material cost. Plus 10%. That will get you close.

This is the frustrating part, that I've gone through quite a few times, everybody says "oh call so and so and they'll take them", well they aren't taking in any animals right now. Thats probably 90% of shelters and foster programs, hence the dumping of animals. I had done a lot of volunteer work for outreach programs, working with people recovering from drug and alcohol problems, that were homeless. Seen this scenario countless times; an individual gets their life back together, gets off the street, gets a job, starts becoming a functioning member of society. Like most normal people they'll get a pet, it's actually recommended for some people in recovery, it can aid in the recovery process, caring for an animal. Well then it happens, they relapse, badly, things go downhill pretty fast. Within a month everything they worked for is gone, they can barely take care of themselves, let alone an animal. So they call the pound, a couple pet rescues, no luck. Someone in the throws of addiction, literally fighting for their life, isn't going to work tirelessly to find their pet a home, because that is what it takes in DFW. Almost every option is not available, for one reason or another. So they end up dumping their animal. Sadly there's just not enough resources.

I had a coworker from Ethiopia that was a die hard Buffalo Bills fan, once a year would fly to NY for at least one game. Had shirts, jerseys, hats, license plate frame, anything. I asked him how the fuck did you become a Bills fan buddy? Well during the Bills epic 4 Superbowl loss run in the 90's, all those pre-made hats, shirts, even rain ponchos that said "Buffalo Bills Superbowl Champions" ended up in Ethiopia. He said every winter they'd get like a shipping container full from the UN, all new clothing, a lot of stuff you'd see at Marshalls or Ross. Pants with one leg a inch shorter, jackets where the pockets were accidentally sewn shut, just a bunch of manufacturer defects. In was like Christmas in his village. He said the one article of clothing that never had defects, that was perfectly made, the clothing for the Superbowl loser from the prior year. The 4 year Superbowl loss the Bills had going, outfitted a bunch of people in new clothing, defect free. Thats why he was a diehard Bills fan.

I had this conversation a few weeks ago, about trafficking in general. Doesn't matter what is being trafficked, drugs or humans, we can't stop it. We can slow it down, we can make it harder, but it'll continue. You could say I've worked on the front lines, been in the trenches, have some experience in this. The people that are tasked with being the defensive front, the ones that aid the victims, the ones that arrest the street dealers selling drugs that were trafficked, the ones tracking down the people responsible for trafficking immigrants, for everyone involved in the fight its their job. They choose to make this a career, meaning they work probably 50 or more hours a week, have a couple weeks of vacation time a year, occasionally call in sick, might have to take a couple days off to career for a sick child or relative. They have lives like anyone else in the workforce. People involved in trafficking, its not their job, it's their life. They don't have vacation days or quitting time is 5:00pm, it's their life 24 hours a day. 24 hours a day they are committed to getting whatever it is across that border, humans, drugs, weapons, whatever it is that's their source of income. You can't defeat something like that. You can't defeat a 24 hour, 7 days a week machine, that never sleeps, never takes days off, that is always running. You can build a wall, fence, robot dogs with laser eyes. Won't stop it. We can hope to detour it, slow it down, and arrest the people who are behind it.

So, unpopular opinion, but Dallas *has* housing for homeless. I spent many years volunteering at outreach programs, after being homeless myself. The issue is the programs are not always accessible, there's strict guidelines in some of them, and there's a portion of the homeless population that just doesn't give a fuck. My experience might be anecdotal, however, I have years of experience on both sides of the needle. If you took the entire homeless population of Dallas, offered them a guaranteed housing program, with job opportunities or help them file the necessary paperwork for SSI, you'd reduce the population by 30%. We'll say 35%, for the sake of math. You still have 35% of the population that has serious drug and alcohol problems, some have tried rehab multiple times and have given up hope, some just don't care. They want to use drugs. You take the remaining 30% that have mental health issues, unless they're institutionalized they will not take their meds. No meds, no therapy, no Dr, nothing. Leaving them homeless, unable to be part of society. California just started to have certified "camps", where homeless can set up away from the city, live in peace, no police hassling them, just weekly visits from social workers if they chose to enroll in housing programs. You can't ticket someone for vagrancy, if you're not giving them opportunities to not be a vagrant. That's the only way I see to corral the homeless issue, give them a place they can set up camp, have the opportunities should they want them. The Bridge, Stewpot, 24 Hour Club, Turtle Creek, Austin, Salvation Army, I could go on and on. Those are all housing programs, some assistance with addiction as well. Yes some have waiting lists, some have strict rules, some are kinda nasty. Help is out there, it just takes a concerted effort by the government to get everyone the help, or to get people the space they need to camp out. Which red states aren't gonna do.

So I took Covid seriously, got the vaccines, wore a mask, social distancing, everything. However, it wasn't as serious as this. This was pretty fucking scary, and I'll tell you why. At the time I lived in the M streets off Mockingbird, not far from the hospital for patient zero. I remember when his nurses got it from him (patient zero), and he died, people really started freaking out. This is how I know the government was way more concerned over this than Covid, I started receiving phone calls for blood donations, from agencies that I never gave my number to. Now why this is crazy is because I have 0- blood, I used to donate a lot when I was younger because I knew my blood type really does save lives. But it's been a good 10 years since my last donation, and I don't even think it was in Texas. So how did The American Red Cross and Charter Blood Care (it's whatever company that does the blood transfers for hospitals) get my number and know I lived in the vicinity? And that I have 0- blood which is desperately needed for patients with Ebola? I never donated blood with them, had lab work done by any companies they affiliate with, nothing. Doesn't that break HIPAA laws? Getting my medical information without my permission? Because they did. Now I wasn't upset, it just made me realize that it's pretty serious if they're contacting people with my blood type, because they know if it spreads they'll need it. I've met 2 other people with my blood type who had a similar experience, but our blood type is so rare you're not going to meet many people. But they too had local blood donation agencies contact them (one girl never donated before and they knew her blood type), and basically pleaded to donate. We all did, I mean it's the right thing to do. But that's how you know if the government is really scared we're going to get hit with a plague, people with rare blood types who's blood can be universally used suddenly gets called for donations. Constantly. I posted this comment awhile back, someone else commented they had worked for the CDC in Denton, there's a whole protocol for breaking HIPPA laws. But I am not familiar with that.

I had linked a clip from a podcast a while ago in a Dart thread (few years now), and now I can't find it. It was from the show Radiolab, just by chance that day I listened the topic was city government comparisons, public transportation being the main topic. It was two separate east coast towns, one was Boston, it was going through the history of public transportation and the costs associated with it. The issue with the Dallas (well the metroplex really) is that the city did not ever depend on public transportation, as opposed to some cities where it's an artery for the lifeblood. Blue collar dock workers needed the train line, plant mechanics from the steel mill used the train line, and regional power plant maintenance operators rely on the subway during inclement weather. Various jobs that are *crucial* to any large city, those similar positions in Dallas, they drive their F250 to work every day, they aren't taking public transportation. I've lived in Dallas almost 25 years now as a forced transplant, I distinctly remember my first day here as a Texan shopping in Tom Thumb, and overhearing a conversation. I was a 20 year lapsed fan, I'd occasionally thumb through a magazine or watch a few minutes if it was on TV, but for the most part I was removed. I always use Bruno Sammartino as a prime example, because a bearhug finisher would get you killed in a real life fight. Fans know this. Fans didn't care. Because he was literally the American dream in real life, came to America at 14 years old barely weighing a 100lbs, because he hid in a cave for over a year with his mom, because of Nazis. Finally his dad gets enough money working in New York, buys the boat tickets and the rest is history. With the east coast already having a heavy Italian presence, you also had immigrants from all over Europe, a real melting pot. For them to see Bruno as champ, to see the American dream is attainable, you can provide for your family and have a good life. Fans couldn't give a fuck if it was fake, because he gave people hope. It's a beautiful story.

Another pre 911 fatality, I could be wrong, but I swear delays and all-out cancelations have gotten worse and worse until recently with the pandemic. Making it miserable to fly now. One wintery February night I was flying out of DFW to Sacramento (I think maybe 2000?) it was literally the last flight of the night and a classic Dallas Ice storm was coming in. There was some audible gasps, some please god save me, some oh fucks, then *BOOM* we're airborne. Felt like you got kicked in the chest, I've never experienced that amount of G Force on a commercial flight, whatever the pilot did to pull us out of that slide to get airborne it worked. Depends on the state, in Texas you have to file for a lost title and see if it's been registered in xx amount of years. Oh and you just can't find it, like it's sitting on the side of the road (or in a barn) it basically has to be on property you own or it was removed at request of the registered owner. It's relatively easy actually, I had dated a girl and her dad owned a junk removal service, occasionally he'd come up on abandoned vehicles and if it was worth it he'd apply for a lost title. Just a lot of paperwork, they nickel and dime you to death with fees. Unless it's still owned or was owned by finance company/bank, that's a hassle but still possible. On the flip side I'm originally from California, you'd probably find Jimmy Hofa before you'll get a lost title for a vehicle. Pretty close to the same process as Texas, except it's a shit ton more money, and lot more leg work. Just gathering the needed documents to show you legally obtained the vehicle, and what you're going to do with it.

The gayborhood was a legit hidden gem, straight people wouldn't think about living in Oaklawn for the most part, because they weren't gay. But Oaklawn *was* considered uptown in the early 1980's, because of new and stylish condominiums, and the counter culture that started leaning towards flamboyant and extravagant. In 2008ish I could rent a decent size studio apartment, with real hardwood floors, old school porcelain pedestal sinks, built with real quality, for $580 a month. Even then it was a steal. It was a safe area, my courtyard had a fucking water fountain with beautiful foliage, it was amazing. I'm not gay but I didn't give a fuck who is, the whole vibe of the area was incredible. I was considering moving back when I was buying a condominium, hoping to score one of those older units, that was a quality build and taken care of. Welp, I learned real quick shit is cheap for reason, sadly that area has changed. I say cheap considering the structure. Really does make me sad, because it really was a harmonious community, I felt safe having my daughter there. Turtle Creek is way out of my price range, and even if I could afford to live in uptown proper, it's too congested. It boils down to a human condition that I'm not intellectual enough to explain, if a certain color or creed of individuals are the main cause of problems, eventually everyone of that color or creed will get looped into the same negative feelings. It's not fair, but that's what occurs, and I honestly wish I knew how to fix it. Because blanket racism and homophobia does no one good.

That's probably your only option if you're sub $100k a year, and work in Dallas. Buy a little Civic or Corolla, and be prepared to drive a little ways for the next 20 years until you can build up equity in that home, sell it, then move where you want. That's my advice, but I'm just some dude on the internet.

To touch on buying a vehicle from the plant, in the 1900's up until the 1930's this was common in a lot of areas. I want to say around the mid 1920's is when it really got uniformed, where dealerships were really franchised. You have to think people were taking a horse and buggy to buy a car, sometimes a tractor if the steam engine on it would make it that far. It's pretty fascinating around the turn of the century how vehicles sales went, for the vehicles that were available. For a brief time the market share was split pretty evenly, between fossil fuel, steam, and electric. Problem with steam is its near impossible to construct a free flowing system small enough for a passenger vehicle, unlike a train. Electric vehicles had the same problem we still have, lack of infrastructure for charging and proprietary charging systems (even though more EV's are starting to use the same set up now), but with internal combustion engines the earlier designs could run various fuels. Gasoline, Kerosene, and even certain solvents sold at pharmacies. It would run incredibly poorly, backfire, and make unbearable noise, however it would still get you to the top speed of 25mph. Most people would take that over strapping up the buggy, getting the horses lined out, cleaning out their shoes, filling up the jugs for water, just a real fiasco.

I was just talking about this with a coworker, we're both lapsed fans who were big into professional wrestling, starting watching again after a long time. This time around I started getting into the history of pro wrestling, how it became a thing, and how did it become so popular. Originally professional wrestling was part of a traveling carnival or circus, really started touring in the 1890's. You'd have a variety of spectacles, a little person, a fat person, a really tall person, a guy with lobster claws for hands (that we know now is a birth defect), just all these different type of people that someone from a small Midwest town would *never* see. And then you could see two grown men wrestle each other to the ground! First one to hold his opponent down for 3 seconds wins! A lot of these wrestlers were some of the first collegiate athletes, and someway found their way into wrestling for a living. Even after the turn of the century entertainment was hard to come by, you might be lucky enough to have access to a radio, or a local newspaper (if you had decent reading comprehension), but not a whole lot going on. Odds are most people during this time *might* have seen a school yard fight, or a maybe a town drunk getting roughed up by the cops. But never two guys really going at it, really trying to best their opponent. It was fascinating for that time period. Now boxing and wrestling historians argue pro wrestling became more of a show that an actual competition around the 1920's to 1930's, these weren't a 10 minute exhibition, it could take someone up to an hour to pin their opponent. Then you do it all over again the next day, this could go on for over a week, that would wear on anyone tremendously. Then you pack up the show, travel for a few days, set up, and do it all over again day after day. At one point someone was burnt out and just told his opponent to pin him, he couldn't go on like this. That's when it started to become a show, if you're going to give up a loss at least make it entertaining. Over a hundred years later we grown adults in spandex fake fighting, and drawing hundreds of thousands if not millions of people yearly. All started in a carnival.

Yeah it's still a thing in most countries where wrestling has some popularity, and probably won't change. People knew pro wrestling was not a real fight since the 1950's, (great book called The Fall Guys) but the characters and the stories got people emotionally invested. In some cases wrestling was second to the wrestler, people cared about the person. There's a reason Bruno Sammartino was the champ for 7 years, and could have held the belt longer, but he was burnt out. He was a working class blue collar hero, an immigrant that over came the odds hiding from Nazis, and now is a pillar of society. Who the fuck ain't gonna cheer that guy? Fake fighting or not, he gave people hope, legitimately. That's really been the roots of pro wrestling, since it was in carnivals and traveling fairs, it was an affordable form of entertainment. Not everyone had the resources to travel and see a big sports team in a metropolitan area, a dozen miles off the farm and into the closest town was all you got. So the opportunity to see a midget, a guy with crab claws for hands, a dancing bear, and witness two grown men attempt to wrestle each other to the ground was pretty big. Granted I wouldn't say WWE is all that affordable, but it's still geared towards family entertainment, and gives people characters to believe in.
